Creating Fixed-Choice Test Items: Matching Exercises

Matching test items are also selection items specially used to measure a student's ability to identify the relationship
between a set of similar items, each of which has two components.

Advantages Matching Exercises

       Ease of construction
       Measure a large amount of related factual material in a relatively short time

Limitations of Matching Exercises

       Restricted to the measurement of factual information
       Highly susceptible to the presence of irrelevant clues
       Difficulty of findings homogenous material

                                                    Lecture: 24

Suggestions for Constructing Matching Exercises

       Use only homogeneous material in the single matching exercise
       Include an unequal number of responses and premises
       Arrange the list of responses in logical order
       Indicate the directions the basis for matching the responses

                                                    Lecture: 25

Forms of Supply Type

       Short answers
       Completion items

They only differ in form of presentation. Short answers are presented in the form of direct questions while completion
items are incomplete statements.

Both of them can be answered with a word, phrase, number, or symbol.

                                                    Lecture: 26

Advantages of Short Answer/Completion Questions

       Teacher wants to control the possibility of guessing
       Teacher wants students to complete a large number of items in a fairly short time
       The possibility of guessing the correct answers to these questions is greatly reduced when compared with true-
        false questions

Disadvantages

       Difficult to frame questions for one specific answer
       Not usable to measure complex learning outcomes

                                                    Lecture: 27

Suggestions for Constructing Short Answer/Completion Questions

Constructed Response Test Items

Subjective test items (essay questions) are constructed response type questions that can be the best way to measure the
students' higher order thinking skills. Such as applying, organizing, synthesizing, integrating, evaluating, or projecting.

Essay type questions are divided into two types

    1. Restricted Response Items
    2. Extended Response Items

Examples:

        Analysis of relationship.
        Compare and contrast positions.
        Explain cause-effect relationship

Guidelines for Constructing Restricted Response Essay Type Items

        Prepare a tentative scoring key in advance
        Do not employ optional questions
        Verify a question‘s quality by writing a trial response to the question
        Evaluate essay responses anonymously
        Specify the value and an approximate time limit for each question

                                                      Lecture: 29

Advantages of essay type items (Extended response questions)

        Effective for assessing higher order abilities
        Comparatively less time consuming
        Emphasizes essential communications skills

Scoring Rubrics provide two benefits

        They support the examination to the extent to which the specified criteria has been reached.
        They provide feedback to students concerning how to improve their performance

Types of Scoring Rubrics

        The analytic (scoring key, point or rating) method
          The analytic scoring requires developing a list of major elements that students are expected to include in an
            ideal answer of a question
          Decide the number of points awarded to students when they include each element
          When assigning number to each element, be sure the total points should match with the essay‘s total value
        The holistic (also called global, sorting or rating) method
          The holistic scoring rubric requires making a judgment about the overall quality of each student‘s response
            to an item.
          No need to mark each specific content element that a student included in the answer.

Topic- 001: Measurement, Assessment and Evaluation
Measurement
Measurement is the process by which the attributes or dimensions of some object (both physical and
abstract) are quantified. The tools used for this purpose may include test, observation, checklist,
homework, portfolios, project etc. Measurement can be easily understood if we use this word to measure
height and distance because these things are physical present in the existence so height can easily be
measured by scale. But in the field of education, our variable are not physical and cannot be directly
measured e.g. attitude, behavior, and achievement etc. these all are abstract, so there measurement is
relatively difficult than those who have physical existence. The tool used for measuring the abstract
variables cannot measure exactly like scale (thermometer). So, in this whole course, whenever the
measurement word is used it means that tool which will be used for measuring student abilities and then
converts it in numerical form.

Assessment
It means an appraisal of something to improve the quality of teaching and learning process for deciding
what more can be done to improve the teaching, learning and outcomes.

Evaluation
Evaluation is the process of making a value judgment against intended learning outcomes and behavior, to
decide the quality and extent of learning. Evaluation is always related to your purpose, you aligned your
purpose of teaching with what students achieved at the end, with their quality and quantity of learning.

Example:
In a classroom situation, as a teacher, when you teach a chapter or unit to a class, first you made the
objectives, either you will do it yourself as a teacher or you take it from a curriculum document of the
particular subject. Objectives are also written at the start of the chapter or book which shows that at the
end of the unit what the student will be able to do this, that is also referred as student learning outcomes.
These SLOs can be checked by two aspects:
       1. Assessment 2.
       Evaluation.

When you, as a teacher reflect on your teaching on a daily basis that what you teach yesterday was a good
way to teach or not, what i taught was the students need, did they understand what I teach, and then you
can decide changing which things can cause the improvement in the learning process of students. This is
known as ASSESSMENT. At the end of the assessment, opinion is not about the individual, it is about the
process from which the students or individuals are passing for the betterment of that process. Evaluation
is that when the learning process is complete and you want to see what are your targets or objectives and
how much my students achieved those objectives, then the tools are made and measures come from that
tell that how much your student learn and what is the quality of their learning.

Difference in Measurement, Assessment and Evaluation
These terms are not different words for same concept, but a process, serving as prerequisite to each other
and having unique purpose. Every mechanism or process starts with the measurement. In the field of
education, measurements generate tools, i.e. test, observation, quiz, checklist, homework and portfolios.
They can give information about students’ learning. The information we got from the tool is
MEASUREMENT. Now if that measurement is used for the process of making the teaching learning
process better than it is ASSESSMENT.
EVALUATION
It is a systematic determination of a subject's merit, worth and significance, using criteria governed by a
set of standards
Assessment and Evaluation don‘t exist in a hierarchy; they both are parallel and different in purpose.
Measurement is the source to move towards assessment and evaluation because it provides the base and
evidence to quantify the teaching learning process. The quantified number has no meaning until we do an
assessment or evaluation. Assessment purpose is to make the teaching learning process better so that
student learning improves and measurement purpose is to align the learning with a purpose.

Topic – 002: Classroom Assessment
The process of gathering, recording, interpreting, using and communicating information about a child's
progress and achievement during the development of knowledge, concepts, skills and attitudes is called
classroom assessment.
When we are teaching in a classroom, we are doing four things:
    1. Developing students ‘knowledge
    2. Improving their concepts
    3. Teaching the skills
    4. Making their attitudes
And while doing so, we collect information about the development of these things, and then we record,
interpret and use it to communicate about the learning progress of students. This whole procedure is
called classroom assessment Classification of Assessment

One of the tools used by teachers to develop a blueprint for the test is called ―table of
specification; in the other word table of specification is a technical name for the blue print of the

   2. Question: Concept of Table of Specification?
    It helps a teacher in allotting the questions to different content areas and Bloom‘s
      learning categories in a systematic manner.
    The blueprint is meant to ensure content validity. Content validity is the most important
      factor in constructing an achievement test. (will be discussed in later unit)
    A unit test or comprehensive exam is based on several lessons and/or chapters in a book
      supposedly reflecting a balance between content areas and learning levels (objectives).
   3. Question: Split Half test?

Split Half Method

Split half method is a measure of internal consistency.

It gives test once. Score two equivalent halves of test, correct correlation between halves to fit
whole test by spearman –brown formula.

Split half reliabilities tend to be higher than equivalent form reliabilities because split half
method is based on the administration of single assessment.

Inter-rater method is a measure of consistency of ratings.

 It gives a set of student’s responses requiring judgmental scoring to two or more raters and has
them independently score the responses.

   6. Question: Dok (depth of knowledge)?

Depth of Knowledge (DOK) DOK (Depth of Knowledge) was presented by Webb in 1997,
giving four levels of learning activities.

Levels of Depth of Knowledge (DOK):

1. Recall

2. Skill/Concept

3. Strategic Thinking

4. Extended Thinking

DOK measures the degree to which the knowledge brings about from students on assessments is
as complex as what students are expected to know and do as stated in the curriculum.

Levels of DOK (Depth of Knowledge):

   1. Recall:

Recall of a fact, information, or procedure. The subject matter at this particular level usually involves
working with facts, terms and/or properties of objects. Key words: list, enlist, name, define etc. 2. 2. 2.
2. Skill/Concept:

It includes the engagement of some mental processing beyond recalling or reproducing a
response. Use information or conceptual knowledge, two or more steps, not just recalling Key
words: Graph, separate, relate, contrast, narrate, compare etc.

3 . Strategic Thinking:

Items falling in this category demand a short-term use of higher order thinking processes, such as
analysis and evaluation, to solve real-world problems with predictable outcomes. Key words:
Argue, critique, formulate.

4. Extended Thinking:

Learning outcomes to this level demand extended use of higher order thinking processes such as
synthesis, reflection, assessment and adjustment of plans over time. Key words: create
synthesize, design and reflection.

Q. Define distractor (Topic 68)

A distractor is an incorrect answer option in a multiple-choice question designed to appear
plausible to students who do not know the correct answer. It serves to differentiate between
students who have mastered the material and those who have not.

Q. Two uses of true and false? (Topic 71)
For measuring such relatively simple learning outcomes, a single declarative statement is used
with anyone of several methods of responding. One of the most useful functions of true and false
items is in measuring the students’ ability to distinguish fact from opinion. Another aspect of
understanding that can be measured by true and false item is ability to recognize cause and effect
relationship. This type of item usually contains true propositions in one statement, and the student
is to judge whether the relationship between them is true or false.

Q. How can true-false items test both cause-effect relationships and logic?

True-false items can be used to assess logical reasoning and cause-effect relationships by requiring
students to analyze the correctness of statements and the relationships between concepts.

Q. What are the advantages of multiple-choice questions (MCQs)? (Topic 73)

   ❖        They allow broad content coverage.
   ❖        They provide objective and reliable scoring.
   ❖        They can assess higher-order thinking skills when well-designed.

Q. Advantages of Alternative Form (True-False) (Topic 73)
True-false questions are well suited for testing lower level learning outcomes, like a student‘s
ability to;
         Identify the correctness of factual statements, e.g. Earth is a planet.
         Definition of terms e.g. Photosynthesis is the process by which leaves make food for plants.
         Statement of principles, e.g. Earth is revolving around the sun.
         Distinguish facts from opinion, e.g. Islam is the official religion of Pakistan.
         Recognize cause-and-effect relationship

   i.       All learning outcomes cannot be measured through alternative form questions. They

   ii.      Ease of guessing correct answers when the answer is not known. With only two
            choices\ (true or false) the student could expect to guess correctly on half of the items
            for which correct answers are not known.

Most publishes achievement test are called standardized achievement tests. These typically are
norm referenced tests. Quite a few criterion referenced achievement tests are also been

Achievement tests are used as part if broader assessment system or alone. They provide

Standard content and procedure makes it possible to give an identical test to individuals in

Q. Issues in test administration

      1. Cheating
      2. Poor testing conditions
      3. Test anxiety
      4. Errors in test scoring procedure.
Q. Guideline for writing essay type

Following guidelines are for writing essay type items when developing a test.
          i.  Frame questions so that the examinee‘s task is explicitly defined.
         ii.  Specify the value and an approximate time limit for each question.
        iii.  Do not employ optional questions.
        iv.   Employ a larger number of questions that require relatively shorter answers rather
              than only a few questions that require long answers.
         v.   Verify a question‘s quality by writing a trial response to the question.
        vi.   Prepare a tentative scoring key in advance of considering examinee responses.
       vii.   Score all answers to one question before scoring the next question.
      viii.   Make prior decisions regarding treatment of such factors as spelling and
              punctuation.

Q. Uses of matching exercise

The typical matching exercise is limited to measuring factual information, based on simple
associations.
It is a compact and efficient method of measuring such simple knowledge outcomes.
It is also being used with pictorial materials in relating pictures and words to identify positions
on maps, charts and diagrams. Regardless of the dorm of presentation, the student‘s task is
essentially to relate two things that have logical association. This restricts the use of matching
exercise to small area of student‘s achievement.

A system of number or values assigned to a work often combines with a level of performance.
High numbers are for best performance like 4, 5 or 6 whereas down to 1 or 0 are the lowest score
in a performance assessment.

   Q. What is difficulty in IRT

   The application of Item difficulty in IRT is defined as the ability at which the probability of
   success on the item is .5 on a logit scale, which is also known as threshold difficulty. An
   item that has a high level of difficulty will be less likely to be answered correctly by an
   examinee with low ability than an item that has a low level of difficulty (i.e., an easy item).

declarative statement is used with anyone of several methods of
responding. One of the most useful functions of true and false items is in
measuring the students’ ability to distinguish fact from opinion. Another
aspect of understanding that can be measured by true and false item is
ability to recognize cause and effect relationship. This type of item
usually contains true propositions in one statement, and the student is to
judge whether the relationship between them is true or false.

small area of student‘s achievement.

For measuring such relatively simple learning outcomes, a single
declarative statement is used with anyone of several methods of
responding. One of the most useful functions of true and false items is in
measuring the students’ ability to distinguish fact from opinion. Another
aspect of understanding that can be measured by true and false item is
ability to recognize cause and effect relationship. This type of item
usually contains true propositions in one statement, and the student is to
judge whether the relationship between them is true or false.
Q. Advantages of Alternative Form (True-False) (Topic 73)
   1. True-false questions are well suited for testing lower level learning
      outcomes, like a student‘s ability to; i. Identify the correctness of
      factual statements, e.g. Earth is a planet.
   2. ii. Definition of terms e.g. Photosynthesis is the process by which
      leaves make food for plants.
   3. iii. Statement of principles, e.g. Earth is revolving around the sun.
   4. iv. Distinguish facts from opinion, e.g. Islam is the official religion
      of Pakistan.
   5. v. Recognize cause-and-effect relationship
Q. 3 limitations of true false (Topic 73)
Most commonly observed limitations are:

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                               Page 1

   i.     All learning outcomes cannot be measured through alternative
          form questions. They are generally limited to lower level
          learning outcomes.
   ii.    Ease of guessing correct answers when the answer is not known.
          With only two choices\ (true or false) the student could expect
          to guess correctly on half of the items for which correct answers
          are not known.
   iii.   There is sometimes a tendency to take quotations from the text
          with a minor change in wording.
   iv.    There may also be a tendency to include trivial material from
          the text.
   v.     True-false items are prone to high guessing and can only be
          used for measuring lower level learning outcomes
Q. Suggestions for true false (Topic 75)
Most important task in formulating statements is free from ambiguity
and irrelevant clues. There are list of things to avoid when phrasing the
statement
         Avoid trivial statements
         Avoid the use of negative especially double negative
    statements.
         Avoid long and complex sentences.
         Avoid including two ideas in one statement unless cause and
    effect relationship are being measured.
Q. short note on matching column? (Topic 82)
The matching type exercises consist of two parallel columns, first
column premises and the second one is responses and the directions for
matching the two columns. Matching test items are also selection items
specially used to measure a student's ability to identify the relationship

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                              Page 2

between a set of similar items, each of which has two components. Such
as words and their definitions, symbols and their meanings, dates and
events, people and their accomplishments, etc. Matching exercise is
economical methods when used with content which has the sufficient
homogeneous factual information. In developing matching items, there
are two columns of material. Matching exercise is used when measuring
a student's ability to identify the relationship between a set of similar
items, each of which has two components.
Q. Uses of matching exercise (Topic 82)
The typical matching exercise is limited to measuring factual
information, based on simple associations. It is a compact and efficient
method of measuring such simple knowledge outcomes. It is also being
used with pictorial materials in relating pictures and words to identify
positions on maps, charts and diagrams. Regardless of the dorm of
presentation, the student‘s task is essentially to relate two things that
have logical association. This restricts the use of matching exercise to
small area of student‘s achievement.
Q. Advantages of matching exercises (Topic 83)
         The major objective of matching exercise is its compact
    form, which makes it possible to measure a large amount of related
    factual material in a relatively short time.
         Another advantage is ease of construction. Poor matching
    items can be rapidly constructed, but good matching item requires
    a high degree of skills.
Q. 3 limitations of matching exercises (Topic 83)
        It is restricted to the measurement of factual information,
    based on rote learning.

        It is highly susceptible to the presence of irrelevant clues.
        Difficulty of findings homogenous material that is significant
    from the viewpoint of our objectives and learning outcomes
Q. Define short questions (Topic 88)
There are two types of item formats which are included in the category
of supply type: short answers and completion and fill in the blanks,
under the range of objective test items. Both the short answers and
completion items are forms of supply item that can be answered by a
word, phrase, number or symbol. They only differ in form of
presentation. Short answers are presented in the form of direct questions
while completion items are incomplete statements. Both of them can be
answered with a word, phrase, number, or symbol. Such items are
frequently used for measuring knowledge of terminology, specific facts,
principles and procedures etc.

Question ⁉️

How does the strategic use of assessment enhance the classroom instructions to promote effective learning outcomes for students? Share specific examples that highlight the positive impact assessment have had on teaching and learning?

Answer

The strategic use of assessment plays a crucial role in enhancing classroom instruction and promoting effective learning outcomes for students. By providing valuable feedback on student understanding, progress, and areas for improvement, assessment guides teachers in tailoring their instruction to meet the diverse needs of their learners.

*Benefits of Strategic Assessment in the Classroom*

1. *Identifying Student Strengths and Weaknesses:* Assessment allows teachers to pinpoint individual student strengths and weaknesses, enabling them to provide targeted support and enrichment activities.

2. *Guiding Instructional Decisions:* Assessment data informs teachers about the effectiveness of their teaching methods and helps them make informed decisions about lesson planning, pacing, and differentiation.

3. *Promoting Student Self-Assessment:* Engaging students in self-assessment activities fosters metacognition, enabling them to reflect on their own learning, identify areas for growth, and set goals for improvement.

4. *Monitoring Student Progress:* Regular assessment provides ongoing feedback on student progress, allowing teachers to track individual growth and identify students who may need additional support or intervention.

5. *Enhancing Communication and Collaboration:* Assessment can serve as a basis for communication and collaboration between teachers, parents, and students, promoting a shared understanding of student learning and progress.

*Examples of Assessment Strategies and Their Impact*

1. *Exit Tickets:* Brief assessments at the end of a lesson, such as quick quizzes or writing prompts, provide immediate feedback on student comprehension and allow teachers to address any misconceptions before moving on.

2. *Formative Assessment Techniques:* Techniques like observation, questioning, and peer review offer ongoing insights into student understanding and engagement, enabling teachers to adapt their instruction in real-time.

3. *Performance-Based Assessments:* Projects, presentations, and portfolios allow students to demonstrate their understanding in a more holistic and creative manner, providing teachers with a richer understanding of their learning.

4. *Rubrics and Checklists:* Clear and well-defined rubrics and checklists provide students with specific criteria for success, guiding their learning and helping them assess their own progress.

5. *Self-Reflection Activities:* Journal prompts, peer feedback sessions, and reflective discussions encourage students to evaluate their own learning, identify areas for improvement, and set goals for further growth.

The strategic use of assessment is not about simply grading students or producing data for accountability purposes. It is about using assessment as a tool to inform instruction, support student learning, and promote a culture of continuous improvement in the classroom. By embedding assessment into the fabric of teaching and learning, educators can create a more dynamic and responsive learning environment that empowers all students to reach their full potential.

ENG520_Glossary

1. Assessment :Assessment refers to the wide variety of methods or tools that
   educators use to evaluate, measure, and document the academic readiness,
   learning progress, skill acquisition, or educational needs of students.
2. Benchmark :An expected performance level for a student at a particular point in
   time determined by standards based criteria; an identified content standard for a
   particular course, grade level, or developmental level at a specific point in time
3. Constructed Response Questions :Assessment item for which students create
   or produce their own answer or response. Examples of constructed-response
   questions include short answer questions and extended written response/essay
   questions.
4. Formative Assessment :Formative assessments are assessments for learning.
   They are designed to provide information needed to adjust teaching and learning
   while they are happening. These assessments are used by teachers and students
   to determine what students have learned in order to plan further instruction
5. High Stake Assessment :High-stakes assessments are typically standardized
   tests used for the purposes of accountability—i.e., any attempt by federal, state,
   or local government agencies to ensure that students are enrolled in effective
   schools and being taught by effective teachers.
6. Learning objective :A learning objective is a specific statement that describes
   what the student is to learn, understand, or to be able to do as a result of a lesson
   or a series of lessons.
7. Measurement :Measurement is simply the process of assigning a number, or a
   score if you will, to some performance or product. Examples would include
   grading a test or a homework assignment in terms of number or percent of correct
   or incorrect responses.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG520_Glossary

8. Multiple Choice Questions :A task-type in which learners are given a question
   and three or four possible answers or options. They choose the correct answer
   from the options they are given.
9. Norm Referenced Test :Assessments that compare a student’s performance to
   that of other students rather than to previously established criteria. Standardized
   examinations such as the SAT are norm-referenced tests
10. Performance Assessment :Performance assessments are designed to
   measure what students know through their ability to perform certain tasks. In
   certain situations, performance assessments – sometimes called performance-
   based assessments – may provide a more accurate indication of what students can
   do than traditional assessments are able to provide. Performance-based
   assessments typically include exhibitions, investigations, creation of products,
   demonstrations, written or oral responses, journals, and portfolios.
11. Pre-Assessment :Assessments that gather and analyze baseline data about
   what students know and can do as they enter the learning experience.
12. Reliability :Reliability refers to the degree of consistency or dependability of
   a test. A reliable test will produce similar scores and distributions whenever it is
   given to similar populations. Thus, if a student scored a 90 on an achievement
   test today, then, if the test is reliable, the student's score would not differ
   substantially if the test were taken again another day. Reliability may also mean
   that a student would earn similar scores on two different forms of a test, if tested
   at about the same time.
13. Selected Response Question :Assessment item for which students select a
   response from possible responses that are provided. Examples of selected-
   response questions include multiple-choice, true/false, and matching

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG520_Glossary

14. Summative Assessment :Summative assessments are assessments of
   learning. They are designed to document what students have learned at the end
   of a period of instruction relative to the standards.
15. Validity :Validity is a term that describes how well a test, or a test item,
   measures what it claims to measure, accurately predicts a behavior, or accurately
   contributes to decision making about the presence or absence of a characteristic.

   schools and being taught by effective teachers.
6. Learning objective :A learning objective is a specific statement that describes
   what the student is to learn, understand, or to be able to do as a result of a lesson
   or a series of lessons.
7. Measurement :Measurement is simply the process of assigning a number, or a
   score if you will, to some performance or product. Examples would include
   grading a test or a homework assignment in terms of number or percent of correct
   or incorrect responses.

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG520_Glossary

8. Multiple Choice Questions :A task-type in which learners are given a question
   and three or four possible answers or options. They choose the correct answer
   from the options they are given.
9. Norm Referenced Test :Assessments that compare a student’s performance to
   that of other students rather than to previously established criteria. Standardized
   examinations such as the SAT are norm-referenced tests
10. Performance Assessment :Performance assessments are designed to
   measure what students know through their ability to perform certain tasks. In
   certain situations, performance assessments – sometimes called performance-
   based assessments – may provide a more accurate indication of what students can
   do than traditional assessments are able to provide. Performance-based
   assessments typically include exhibitions, investigations, creation of products,
   demonstrations, written or oral responses, journals, and portfolios.
11. Pre-Assessment :Assessments that gather and analyze baseline data about
   what students know and can do as they enter the learning experience.
12. Reliability :Reliability refers to the degree of consistency or dependability of
   a test. A reliable test will produce similar scores and distributions whenever it is
   given to similar populations. Thus, if a student scored a 90 on an achievement
   test today, then, if the test is reliable, the student's score would not differ
   substantially if the test were taken again another day. Reliability may also mean
   that a student would earn similar scores on two different forms of a test, if tested
   at about the same time.
13. Selected Response Question :Assessment item for which students select a
   response from possible responses that are provided. Examples of selected-
   response questions include multiple-choice, true/false, and matching

By ASFAND YARR

                              ENG520_Glossary

14. Summative Assessment :Summative assessments are assessments of
   learning. They are designed to document what students have learned at the end
   of a period of instruction relative to the standards.
15. Validity :Validity is a term that describes how well a test, or a test item,
   measures what it claims to measure, accurately predicts a behavior, or accurately
   contributes to decision making about the presence or absence of a characteristic.

CREATING FIXED-CHOICE TEST ITEMS: TRUE/FALSE AND ITS USES

True/False Items:

       A statement is given, and the test taker marks it as either "true" or "false."
       Example: "The sun rises in the west. True or False?"

Uses of True/False Items:

       Great for quickly assessing basic knowledge, facts, or concepts.
       Used in quizzes, exams, or surveys to check comprehension.

Advantages of True/False Items:

       Quick to write, easy to grade.
       Covers a wide range of material in less time.

Limitations:

       May encourage guessing since there’s a 50% chance of guessing correctly.
       Does not test deeper understanding.

Suggestions for Constructing True/False Items:

       Write clear, straightforward statements.
       Avoid double negatives or tricky wording.
       Make sure only one idea is presented in each statement.

CREATING FIXED-CHOICE TEST ITEMS: MATCHING EXERCISES

Matching Exercises:

       Two columns are presented; students match items from one column to another.
       Example: Column A: Countries, Column B: Capitals.

Uses:

       Useful for testing associations, such as definitions, names, or facts.

       Example: Match authors with their famous works.

Advantages:

       Compact and efficient for testing related concepts.
       Easy to grade.

Limitations:

       May confuse students if options in columns are too similar.
       Can become a guessing game if there are too many options.

Suggestions for Constructing Matching Exercises:

       Keep the lists balanced and related.
       Use clear and concise terms.
       Include extra options to reduce guessing.

CREATING FIXED-CHOICE TEST ITEMS: SHORT QUESTIONS

Short Answer/Completion Questions:

       Students provide brief responses to open-ended prompts.
       Example: "What is the capital of France?"

Uses:

       Ideal for testing factual knowledge or key concepts.

Advantages:

       Encourages recall rather than recognition.
       Easier to write compared to essay questions.

Suggestions for Constructing Short Answer Questions:

       Be specific and clear in the question.
       Avoid ambiguity to ensure accurate responses.
       Indicate the expected length of the answer if necessary.

CREATING CONSTRUCTED RESPONSE TEST ITEMS

Constructed Response Items:

      Students create their answers rather than choosing from given options.

Guidelines for Restricted Response Items:

      Provide clear instructions with specific limitations (e.g., "Explain in 50 words").
      Focus on targeted content to avoid confusion.

CREATING EXTENDED RESPONSE TEST ITEMS

Extended Response Items:

      Open-ended questions requiring detailed, essay-style answers.
      Example: "Discuss the importance of environmental conservation."

Guidelines for Writing Essay Items:

      Use prompts that encourage critical thinking.
      Be clear about the scope and structure of the answer.

Scoring Rubrics for Essay Items:

      Holistic Scoring Rubric: Provides an overall score based on general quality.
      Analytic Scoring Rubric: Breaks the score into specific criteria (e.g., content, grammar).

ANALYZING THE TEST

Item Analysis:

      Examines how individual test items perform, such as their difficulty and discrimination.

Key Concepts:

      Item Difficulty: Measures how easy or hard a question is.
      Item Discrimination: Shows how well an item differentiates between strong and weak students.

Item Response Theory (IRT):

      Advanced approach to analyze test items, focusing on individual performance and item properties.

ADMINISTERING TESTS

        Refers to organizing and conducting tests.
        Steps include assembling, packing, reproducing, and ensuring smooth administration.

Things to Remember:

        Provide clear instructions.
        Prepare backup materials for emergencies.

SCORING TESTS

Scoring Rubric:

        A guide to evaluate and grade responses consistently.

Types:

        Holistic Rubric: Overall impression.
        Analytic Rubric: Breaks down into detailed components (e.g., content, organization).

STANDARDIZED TESTS

Standardized Tests:

        Pre-designed tests given under controlled conditions to measure student achievement.

Characteristics:

        Uniform administration.
        Reliable and valid results.

Criterion-Referenced Interpretation:

        Compares performance to a set standard.

Norm-Referenced Interpretation:

        Compares performance to other test takers.

HIGH STAKES TESTING AND ISSUES

High-Stakes Testing (HST):

         Tests that have significant consequences, such as college admissions.

Issues:

         Pressure on students and educators.
         Risk of focusing too much on test preparation.

Recommendations for Effective HST:

         Align tests with curriculum goals.
         Provide preparation resources for students.

ENG520
Concept of Assessment

Assessment is a systematic process of gathering, analyzing, and interpreting information about a
learner's knowledge, skills, attitudes, or performance. It plays a crucial role in education by
providing feedback to students, teachers, and stakeholders about progress and achievement.
Effective assessment not only measures learning outcomes but also identifies areas for
improvement, shaping instruction and curriculum design.

Measurement, Assessment, and Evaluation

   •   Measurement involves quantifying learner performance using numerical data, such as
       test scores.
   •   Assessment goes beyond measurement by interpreting the data to determine a learner’s
       strengths and weaknesses.
   •   Evaluation is a broader process that uses assessment results to judge the overall
       effectiveness of teaching strategies, curricula, or programs.

Classroom Assessment

Classroom assessment refers to the practices teachers use to evaluate students’ learning within
the classroom setting. These assessments can be informal (e.g., questioning during lessons) or
formal (e.g., quizzes, projects). Classroom assessments are integral to guiding instruction,
providing immediate feedback, and tailoring lessons to meet student needs.

Types of Assessment

Assessments can be categorized as:

   •   Formative Assessment: Conducted during instruction to monitor and improve learning
       (e.g., quizzes, class discussions).
   •   Summative Assessment: Conducted at the end of a learning period to evaluate overall
       achievement (e.g., final exams, standardized tests).

   •   Diagnostic Assessment: Identifies students’ prior knowledge and potential learning
       challenges.
   •   Norm-Referenced Assessment (NRT): Compares a student’s performance to peers.
   •   Criterion-Referenced Assessment (CRT): Measures a student’s performance against a
       predefined standard or objective.

Use of Assessment in Classroom Instruction

Assessment guides classroom instruction by identifying learning gaps and informing teaching
strategies. Formative assessments provide ongoing insights, allowing teachers to adjust their
methods, while summative assessments validate whether instructional goals have been achieved.

Use of Assessment in Classroom Instruction – Formative and Summative
Assessment

   •   Formative Assessment supports learning during the instructional process, encouraging
       continuous improvement.
   •   Summative Assessment certifies learning outcomes at the end of a course or unit,
       focusing on accountability and performance measurement.

Types of Assessment: Methods of Interpreting Results

   •   Quantitative Methods: Provide numerical data (e.g., test scores).
   •   Qualitative Methods: Offer descriptive insights (e.g., observations, portfolios).
       Interpretation involves analyzing these results to make data-driven educational decisions.

Assessment, Testing, and National Curriculum

Assessment and testing align with national curriculum standards to ensure consistency and
fairness across educational institutions. These tools evaluate whether curriculum objectives are
met and identify areas for policy or instructional adjustments.

Role of National Curriculum in Assessment

The national curriculum provides a framework for assessment, outlining clear objectives and
learning outcomes. It ensures that assessments are aligned with educational standards and
promote uniformity across schools.

Connecting All Four Levels in Curriculum

The four levels of curriculum—intended, implemented, experienced, and achieved—are
interconnected. Assessment evaluates whether the intended curriculum (what is planned) aligns
with the implemented curriculum (what is taught) and the achieved curriculum (what students
learn).

Modes of Assessment in Curriculum

Modes of assessment include written tests, oral presentations, practical demonstrations, and
project-based evaluations. These methods assess various cognitive, psychomotor, and affective
skills outlined in the curriculum.

Taxonomies of Educational Objectives and Assessment

Taxonomies provide frameworks for categorizing educational objectives. They guide assessment
design to evaluate not only knowledge but also higher-order thinking and skill application.

Bloom’s Taxonomy and SOLO Taxonomy

   •   Bloom’s Taxonomy categorizes cognitive skills from lower-order (remember,
       understand) to higher-order (analyze, evaluate, create).
   •   SOLO Taxonomy (Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes) emphasizes the quality of
       learning outcomes, progressing from simple (uni-structural) to complex (extended
       abstract).

Depth of Knowledge

Depth of Knowledge (DoK) assesses the complexity of tasks students are asked to perform,
ranging from recall of facts to strategic thinking and extended reasoning.

Bloom’s Taxonomy

Bloom’s framework organizes educational goals into six cognitive levels: knowledge,
comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation.

Revised Version of Bloom’s Taxonomy

The revised version shifts the focus from nouns to verbs (e.g., "analyzing" instead of "analysis")
and includes the categories of "remembering," "understanding," "applying," "analyzing,"
"evaluating," and "creating."

Instructional Objectives

Instructional objectives define what learners should achieve after a lesson or course. They
provide clarity for lesson planning, teaching strategies, and assessment design.

Purpose of Testing

Testing serves multiple purposes, including diagnosing learning needs, certifying achievements,
and evaluating instructional effectiveness. It aids in making informed educational decisions and
policy recommendations.

Educational Decision Making

Assessment and testing data inform decisions about curriculum design, student progression,
teacher effectiveness, and resource allocation. They ensure alignment with educational goals and
standards.

Q. Define the term measurement? (Topic 01)
Measurement is the process by which the attributes or dimensions of some object (both physical
and abstract) are quantified. Measurement can be easily understood if we use this word to measure
height and distance because these things are physical present in the existence so height can easily
be measured by scale. But in the field of education, our variable are not physical and cannot be
directly measured e.g. attitude, behavior, and achievement etc. these all are abstract, so there
measurement is relatively difficult than those who have physical existence. The tool used for
measuring the abstract variables cannot measure exactly like scale (thermometer).
Q. Define the term evaluation (Topic 01)
Evaluation is the process of making a value judgment against intended learning outcomes and
behavior, to decide the quality and extent of learning. Evaluation is always related to your purpose,
you aligned your purpose of teaching with what students achieved at the end, with their quality
and quantity of learning.

Q. Differences btw the maximum performance assessment and typical performance
assessment? (Topic 03)
Maximum performance assessment determines what individuals can do when performing at their
best e.g. assess student in an environment when they exhibit their best performance. Procedure of
this type is concerned with how well individual perform when they are motivated to obtain as high
score as possible. This type of assessment includes aptitude tests and achievement tests. The
second category is a typical performance assessment determines what an individual will do under
natural conditions. This type of assessment includes attitude, interest, personality inventories,
observational techniques and peer appraisal. Here the emphasis is on what students will do rather
than what they can do.

    Measurement is the process by which the attributes or dimensions of some object (both physical and
    abstract) are quantified. Measurement can be easily understood if we use this word to measure height
    and distance because these things are physical present in the existence so height can easily be measured
    by scale. But in the field of education, our variable are not physical and cannot be directly measured
    e.g. attitude, behavior, and achievement etc. these all are abstract, so there measurement is relatively
    difficult than those who have physical existence. The tool used for measuring the abstract variables
    cannot measure exactly like scale (thermometer).

    2. Define concurrent validity?
Concurrent validity This approach allows one to show the test is valid by comparing it with an already
      valid test.

    3. Standards of test?
                      i. Achievement tests
                     ii. Aptitude tests

    4. Formative and summative assessment?

 It determines learning progress, provides feedback to reinforce learning, and correct learning errors. When
we assess student during classroom instruction with a purpose to have a feedback that how can we make
our teacher learning process better, that is formative assessment. In this assessment, we are not assessing
what students learnt or not, rather we assess the process behind the students learning .The process behind
the student learning includes a teaching method, book, if we make all these things according to the needs
of students then learning will improve.
Summative Assessment
It comes at the end of the instructional session (course of the unit). It is designed to measure extend of
achievement of intended learning outcomes. The primary utility of this type of assessment is to assign
grades and certifying the level of mastery and expertise in a certain subject. It is usually done through
teacher made achievement tests or alternative assessment techniques like portfolio to summarize the overall
performance of the student at the end of the session. It is not compulsory to do it at the end of the semester,
in semester system, there is a midterm and final term in one semester, and these both are summative
assessment. It usually compares the student learning either with other students’ learning (norm-referenced)
or the standard for a grade level (criterion-referenced). Summative assessment includes teacher made
survey test, performance, rating scales and product scales.

    5. Advantages of mcqs?
      ▪   Ensure objectivity, reliability and validity; preparations of questions with colleagues provide
          constructive criticism.
      ▪   Increase significantly the range and variety of facts that can be sampled in given time.
      ▪   Provide precise and unambiguous measurement of the higher intellectual processes.

      ▪       Provide detailed feedback for both students and teachers.
      ▪       MCQs are easy and rapid to score.

    7. Define the term table of specification?
One of the tools used by teachers to develop a blueprint for the test is called ―table of specification; in the
        other word table of specification is a technical name for the blue print of the test. It is the first
        formal step to develop a test.

    8. Differences btw the maximum performance assessment and typical performance
       assessment?
Maximum performance assessment determines what individuals can do when performing at their best e.g.
      assess student in an environment when they exhibit their best performance. Procedure of this type
      is concerned with how well individual perform when they are motivated to obtain as high score as
      possible. This type of assessment includes aptitude tests and achievement tests.

The second category is a typical performance assessment determines what an individual will do under
natural conditions. This type of assessment includes attitude, interest, personality inventories, observational
techniques and peer appraisal. Here the emphasis is on what students will do rather than what they can do.
    9. Three suggestions to create mcq ?
          ●     The general applicability and the superior qualities of multiple choice test items are realized
                most fully when care is taken in their construction. This involves formulating clearly stated
                problems, identifying plausible alternatives, and removing irrelevant clues to the answer.
          ●     The item stem should include as much as of the item as possible and should be free of
                irrelevant material. Explanation: Clear stem increase the probability of the item as well as
                reduce the reading time required.
          ●     Try to avoid the negative statements, unless the significant learning outcome requires it.
          ●     An item should contain only one correct or clearly best answer.
          ●     Explanation: Including more than one correct answer in a test item and asking students to
                select all the correct alternatives has 2 shortcomings.
          ●     a. Such items are usually no more than a collection of true and false item presented in MCQ
                form.
          ●     b. The number of alternatives selected as correct answers varies from one student to another.

    10. Key steps in using portfolios.
Specify purpose
Provide guidelines for selecting portfolios
Define student‘s role in selection and self-evaluation.
Specify evaluation criteria.
Use portfolios in instruction and communication.

    11. Define the term evaluation

Evaluation is the process of making a value judgment against intended learning outcomes and behavior, to
        decide the quality and extent of learning. Evaluation is always related to your purpose, you aligned
        your purpose of teaching with what students achieved at the end, with their quality and quantity of
        learning.

    12. Construct validity in text.

    1. Define the term measurement?

    Measurement is the process by which the attributes or dimensions of some object (both physical and
    abstract) are quantified. Measurement can be easily understood if we use this word to measure height
    and distance because these things are physical present in the existence so height can easily be measured
    by scale. But in the field of education, our variable are not physical and cannot be directly measured
    e.g. attitude, behavior, and achievement etc. these all are abstract, so there measurement is relatively
    difficult than those who have physical existence. The tool used for measuring the abstract variables
    cannot measure exactly like scale (thermometer).

    2. Define concurrent validity?
Concurrent validity This approach allows one to show the test is valid by comparing it with an already
      valid test.

    3. Standards of test?
                      i. Achievement tests
                     ii. Aptitude tests

    4. Formative and summative assessment?

 It determines learning progress, provides feedback to reinforce learning, and correct learning errors. When
we assess student during classroom instruction with a purpose to have a feedback that how can we make
our teacher learning process better, that is formative assessment. In this assessment, we are not assessing
what students learnt or not, rather we assess the process behind the students learning .The process behind
the student learning includes a teaching method, book, if we make all these things according to the needs
of students then learning will improve.
Summative Assessment
It comes at the end of the instructional session (course of the unit). It is designed to measure extend of
achievement of intended learning outcomes. The primary utility of this type of assessment is to assign
grades and certifying the level of mastery and expertise in a certain subject. It is usually done through
teacher made achievement tests or alternative assessment techniques like portfolio to summarize the overall
performance of the student at the end of the session. It is not compulsory to do it at the end of the semester,
in semester system, there is a midterm and final term in one semester, and these both are summative
assessment. It usually compares the student learning either with other students’ learning (norm-referenced)
or the standard for a grade level (criterion-referenced). Summative assessment includes teacher made
survey test, performance, rating scales and product scales.

    8. Differences btw the maximum performance assessment and typical performance
       assessment?
Maximum performance assessment determines what individuals can do when performing at their best e.g.
      assess student in an environment when they exhibit their best performance. Procedure of this type
      is concerned with how well individual perform when they are motivated to obtain as high score as
      possible. This type of assessment includes aptitude tests and achievement tests.

The second category is a typical performance assessment determines what an individual will do under
natural conditions. This type of assessment includes attitude, interest, personality inventories, observational
techniques and peer appraisal. Here the emphasis is on what students will do rather than what they can do.

                            SUBJECTIVE PART (from file)

   1. Levels of Depth of Knowledge (DOK)?

DOK (Depth of Knowledge) was presented by Webb in 1997, giving four levels of
learning activities. 1) Recall: Simple recall of facts (e.g., define, list). 2)
Skill/Concept: Application of concepts or procedures (e.g., compare, summarize).
3) Strategic Thinking: Reasoning, planning, using evidence (e.g., analyze,

critique). 4) Extended Thinking: Complex reasoning over time (e.g., design,
synthesize, reflect).

   2. What is Split Half Method?

Split half method is a measure of internal consistency. Split half reliabilities tend to
be higher than equivalent form reliabilities because split half method is based on
the administration of single assessment. The split- d is a way to check how reliable
a test is by dividing it into two parts and comparing the results. You take one test
and split it into two equal halves, like odd-numbered questions in one half and
even-numbered questions in the other. You score both halves separately. If the
scores on both halves match closely, it means the test is consistent and reliable. The
Spearman Brown formula is then used to adjust the reliability score for the full test.

   3. Differentiate b/w Formative and summative assessment?

Formative Assessment

Formative assessment is used during teaching to monitor students’ learning. It
provides feedback to improve teaching methods and help students overcome
learning difficulties. It focuses on how students are learning, not on grading.

Uses:

   •    Identifies students’ strengths and weaknesses

   •    Helps teachers modify teaching strategies

   •    Improves the teaching–learning process

   •    Encourages students to reflect and improve

Examples:

   •    Class quizzes

   •   Asking questions

   •   Feedback during lessons

Summative Assessment

Summative assessment is conducted at the end of a unit or course to measure
students’ overall achievement. Its main purpose is to evaluate learning outcomes
and assign grades.

Examples:

   •   Final exams

   •   End-of-term tests

   •   Projects

   •   Standardized tests

Key Difference

Formative assessment improves the learning process, while summative
assessment certifies learning achievement.

   4. “Guess Who” Technique?

In this technique the teacher chooses a student’s positive (or negative) behavior as
an example. Other students try to guess which student matches that behavior.
Mostly positive behaviors are used so no one feels bad. This technique is like
nominating classmates, and the score is simply the number of times a student is
mentioned for each behavior. For example:

“Who works well in groups?”

“Who stays calm under pressure?”

Measurement is the process by which the attributes or dimensions of some object (both physical and abstract) are
quantified. Measurement can be easily understood if we use this word to measure height and distance because these things
are physical present in the existence so height can easily be measured by scale. But in the field of education, our variable are
not physical and cannot be directly measured e.g. attitude, behavior, and achievement etc. these all are abstract, so there

                ENG520 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

                 ENG520 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

measurement is relatively difficult than those who have physical existence. The tool used for measuring the abstract
variables cannot measure exactly like scale (thermometer).

Q. Define the term evaluation (Topic 01)

Evaluation is the process of making a value judgment against intended learning outcomes and behavior, to decide the quality
and extent of learning. Evaluation is always related to your purpose, you aligned your purpose of teaching with what
students achieved at the end, with their quality and quantity of learning.

Q. Method of interpreting Results (Topic 02)

    i. Norm Referenced Assessment ii.              Criterion Referenced
    Assessment

Q. Differences btw the maximum performance assessment and typical performance assessment? (Topic 03)

Maximum performance assessment determines what individuals can do when performing at their best e.g. assess student in
an environment when they exhibit their best performance. Procedure of this type is concerned with how well individual
perform when they are motivated to obtain as high score as possible. This type of assessment includes aptitude tests and
achievement tests. The second category is a typical performance assessment determines what an individual will do under
natural conditions. This type of assessment includes attitude, interest, personality inventories, observational techniques and
peer appraisal. Here the emphasis is on what students will do rather than what they can do.

Q. Write four levels in which learning of students is classified OR Role of National Curriculum in Assessment (Topic
07).

In national curriculums of Pakistan, learning of student is classified into four levels.

    1. Competency
    2. Standards
    3. Benchmarks
    4. Student learning outcome (SLOs)
Q. Write three taxonomies. (Topic 10)

    1. Bloom‘s taxonomy of educational objective
    2. Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes (SOLO)
    3. Depth of Knowledge (DOK)
Q. Types of Written Tests (Topic 19)

Verbal: Emphasize reading, writing, or speaking. The most tests in education are verbal tests.

Non-verbal: It does not require reading, writing or speaking ability. The tests composed of numerals or drawings are an
example of non-verbal test.

Objective: It refers to scoring of tests when two or more scorers can easily agree on whether the answer is correct or
incorrect; the test is an objective one. True/ false, multiple choice and matching tests are examples of it

                 ENG520 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

                 ENG520 Midterm Short Notes BY PIN2 and MUHAMMAD (MAS All Rounder)

Subjective: When it is difficult for two scorers to agree on whether an item is correct or incorrect, the test is a subjective
one. Essay tests are the example of it. Teacher Made It is constructed solely by teacher only to be used in the classroom.

This type of test is custom designed according to need and issues related to specific class.

Standardized: Test constructed by measurement experts over a period of years. They are designed to measure broad
national objectives and have a uniform set of instructions that are adhered to during each administration. Mostly it has
tables of norms, to which a student performance may be compared to determine where the student stands in relation to a
national sample of students at the same level of age or grade

Power: Tests with liberal time limits that allow each student to attempt each item. Items tend to be difficult

Speed: Tests with time limits so strict that no one is expected to complete all items. Items tend to be easy.

Q. Objective types of assessment. (Topic 19)

            (1) Matching Test,
            (2) Multiple Choice Test,
            (3) True False Tests,
            (4) Correct/Incorrect Test,
            (5) Simple Recall Test,
            (6) Best Answer Test,
            (7) Completion Test, and
            (8) Classification Test.
Q. Functions of summative assessment (Topic 25)

     Focus of measurement in summative assessment is on course or unit objectives.
     Broad sample of all objectives is used in summative assessment.
     This type of assessment uses wide range of difficulty while selecting items for the test.
     Summative assessment is done at the end of the unit or the course.
     Most important functions of summative assessment is to assign grade, certification of accomplishment and evaluation
       of teaching.
Q. Formative and summative assessment? (Topic 25+26)

It determines learning progress, provides feedback to reinforce learning, and correct learning errors. When we assess
student during classroom instruction with a purpose to have a feedback that how can we make our teacher learning process
better, that is formative assessment. In this assessment, we are not assessing what students learnt or not, rather we assess
the process behind the students learning .The process behind the student learning includes a teaching method, book, if we
make all these things according to the needs of students then learning will improve.

Summative Assessment

Topic - 001: Measurement, Assessment and Evaluation Measurement
What is measurement in the context of education?
Measurement is the process of quantifying attributes or dimensions of objects,
whether physical or abstract, using tools such as tests, observations, checklists,
homework, portfolios, and projects.
Why is measurement in the field of education challenging compared to physical
measurements?
Education deals with abstract variables like attitudes, behaviors, and achievement,
which are not directly measurable like physical objects. Tools used for measuring
these variables cannot measure as precisely as a physical scale or thermometer.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               1

What is the purpose of assessment in education?
Assessment aims to appraise teaching and learning processes to determine how
they can be improved, ultimately enhancing the quality of education.
How does evaluation differ from assessment in education?
Evaluation involves making judgments about the quality and extent of learning in
relation to intended learning outcomes. Assessment focuses on improving the
teaching and learning process, while evaluation examines the achievement of
objectives.
Explain the role of assessment and evaluation in a classroom situation.
Assessment helps teachers reflect on their teaching methods and whether
students are learning effectively. Evaluation is used to measure the quality and
quantity of student learning against specific objectives.
Differentiate between measurement, assessment, and evaluation in education.
Measurement is the process of obtaining information, assessment is about using
this information to improve teaching and learning, and evaluation is about
determining how well students have achieved the learning objectives.
Explain the difference between measurement, assessment, and evaluation.
Measurement involves the process of obtaining information, assessment focuses
on using this information to enhance teaching and learning, and evaluation aims
to determine the quality and quantity of learning against specific objectives.
Topic - 002: Classroom Assessment
What is classroom assessment?
Classroom assessment is the process of gathering, recording, interpreting, using,
and communicating information about a student's progress and achievement in
knowledge, concepts, skills, and attitudes.
How can classroom assessment be classified?
Classroom assessment can be classified based on nature, format, use in classroom
instruction, and method of interpreting results.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                              2

Name the four categories of classroom assessment based on use in classroom
instruction.
The four categories are placement assessment, formative assessment, diagnostic
assessment, and summative assessment.
Topic - 003: Types of Assessment
What are the two types of assessment by nature?
The two types are maximum performance assessment and typical performance
assessment.
What is the focus of maximum performance assessment?
Maximum performance assessment determines what individuals can do when
performing at their best, either to measure past success (achievement) or predict
future success (aptitude).
What is the emphasis of typical performance assessment?
Typical performance assessment focuses on what individuals will do under natural
conditions, often assessing attitudes, interests, personality, and observable
behaviors.
What are the two types of assessment by format?
The two types are fixed choice assessment and complex performance assessment.
Describe maximum performance assessment and its purpose.
Maximum performance assessment assesses what individuals can do when
performing at their best. It is used to measure how well students perform under
optimal conditions, for example, to indicate the degree of success in past learning
activities or to predict success in future learning activities.
Describe complex performance assessment and its applications.
Complex performance assessment is designed to measure performance in real-life
contexts, evaluating tasks and problems valued for their own sake. It involves
hands-on laboratory experiments, projects, essays, and oral presentations, making
it suitable for assessing higher-level skills and abilities.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           3

How is fixed choice assessment different from complex performance
assessment?
Fixed choice assessment uses multiple choice questions, matching exercises, and
other predefined response formats to efficiently measure lower-level knowledge
and skills. Complex performance assessment, on the other hand, assesses
performance in real-life contexts, often using hands-on experiments, projects,
essays, and oral presentations.

Decisions made by teachers based on grades,
influencing students significantly.
What are diagnostic decisions?
Decisions about a student's strengths and weaknesses,
often based on informal teacher-made tests or
standardized tests.
What are placement decisions?
Decisions made after accepting an individual into a
program, determining the best-suited starting point.
Who makes program or curriculum decisions?
These decisions are made at the policy level.
What are administrative decisions?
Decisions made at school, district, state, or national
levels based on measurement data, including financial
decisions.
Topic 019: Types of Test
What are the types of written tests?
Verbal, Non-verbal, Objective, Subjective, Teacher
Made, Standardized, Power, Speed.
What is a verbal test?
Emphasizes reading, writing, or speaking, and most tests
in education are verbal.
Give an example of a non-verbal test.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                     2

Tests composed of numerals or drawings are examples
of non-verbal tests.
What is a teacher-made test?
Constructed solely by a teacher for classroom use,
custom-designed according to specific class needs.
Topic 020: Norm-Referenced Assessment (NRT)
What is the general purpose of assessment?
To gather information for better decision-making.
What is Norm-Referenced Assessment (NRT)?
A type of test that compares a student's performance to
other students, determining their place or rank among a
group.
What does NRT measure?
It provides an estimate of ability in various skills but
tends to be general and less thorough.
How difficult is NRT for students?
It is generally difficult, with only around 50% of students
getting an item right on average.
Topic 021: Criterion-Referenced Assessment (CRT)
What is Criterion-Referenced Assessment (CRT)?
A type of test that tells us about a student's level of
proficiency or mastery of specific skills by comparing
their performance to a standard mastery.
How specific is CRT?
It tends to be specific, measuring a particular set of skills
and focusing on the level of achievement of those skills.
How does CRT compare to NRT in terms of time?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                          3

CRT takes more time as it measures skills more
thoroughly.
What does CRT compare student performance to?
CRT compares student performance to standards
indicative of mastery.
What is the breadth of content sampled in CRT?
Narrow, covering very few objectives.

Lesson 07
      PURPOSE OF TESTING –II
Topic-022: Characteristics of Criterion Referenced Assessment
What is the typical content sampling approach in Criterion Referenced Testing
(CRT)?
CRT usually involves a comprehensive content sampling, often using three or more
items to cover a single objective.
How is the meaning of the score determined in CRT?
The meaning of the score in CRT does not depend on a comparison with other
scores; it directly reflects the connection between the items and the criterion.
What is the emphasis when choosing items in CRT?
Items in CRT are chosen to reflect criterion behavior, emphasizing the domain of
relevant responses.
How is performance measured in CRT, in terms of succeeding or failing?
Performance in CRT is measured by criteria such as achieving proficiency, with
specific percentages (e.g., 90% proficiency) used.
Topic-023: Difference between NRT and CRT Basis of Comparison
What is the main focus of comparison in CRT?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             4

In CRT, the examinee's performance is compared to an external standard of
competence.
How are items selected in CRT compared to NRT?
Answer: CRT items are specific and designed for subject mastery, while NRT items
are of general knowledge nature.
How is success defined in CRT compared to NRT?
In CRT, an examinee is classified as a master or non-master, with no pass/fail limit.
In NRT, success is relative to the performance of other examinees.
What is the difference in average item difficulty between CRT and NRT?
CRT has a higher average item difficulty, expecting mastery, while NRT has a lower
average difficulty, allowing for a broader range of examinee abilities.
How does the score distribution differ between CRT and NRT?
In CRT, the score distribution tends to cluster near the high end, while in NRT, a
broader spread of scores is expected.
What types of scores are commonly reported in CRT and NRT?
Answer: CRT reports focus on classifications like master/non-master or pass/fail,
while NRT commonly uses percentile ranks or scale scores.
Topic-024: Formative Assessment
What is the primary focus of formative assessment?
Answer: Formative assessment provides feedback and information during the
instructional process, while learning is occurring.
Name some types of formative assessment activities.
Answer: Observation during in-class activities, homework exercises, reflections
journals, question and answer sessions, conferences, and in-class activities where
students informally present their results.
How does formative assessment benefit instructors?

3 Suggestions for True/False:

   1. Use clear, simple language.
   2. Avoid double negatives.
   3. Make the statements unequivocally true or false.

5 Suggestions for True/False Items:

   1.   Keep the statement brief and factual.
   2.   Avoid using absolute words like “always” or “never.”
   3.   Include only one main idea in each item.
   4.   Avoid giving clues through length or wording.
   5.   Ensure both true and false items are equal in number and difficulty.

Limitations of True/False:

   1. High chance of guessing correctly (50%).
   2. Difficult to measure higher-order thinking.
   3. May lead to ambiguity if not worded carefully.

2 Uses of True/False:

   1. Assess factual knowledge quickly.
   2. Useful in preliminary or diagnostic testing.

Suggestions to Create True/False Questions:

       Include definite, clear statements.
       Test only one idea per item.
       Use both true and false items in balanced numbers.

Two Suggestions for Construction of True/False:

   1. Avoid trick questions or subtle negatives.
   2. Keep items similar in length to avoid clues.

Advantages of Alternative Form (True/False):

   1. Quick and easy to administer and score.
   2. Covers a wide content range in less time.

3 Suggestions for Matching Exercises:

   1. Use homogeneous content categories.

   2. Keep the list short (5–10 items).
   3. Use more responses than premises to avoid guessing.

5 Suggestions for Matching Exercises:

   1.   Clear instructions should be provided.
   2.   Keep items on one page to avoid back-and-forth.
   3.   Ensure matching items are similar in nature.
   4.   Use logical and meaningful order.
   5.   Avoid grammatical clues.

Explain Matching Exercises (Short and Long):

       Short Matching: Consists of a brief list of premises and options (e.g., vocabulary and
        definitions).
       Long Matching: Includes more detailed sets, possibly using paragraphs or complex ideas
        to match.

Advantages of Matching Exercises:

   1. Efficient for testing recall of related facts.
   2. Easy to grade objectively.
   3. Covers more content in less space.

Limitations of Matching Exercises:

   1. Not suitable for testing deep understanding.
   2. Requires homogenous content, which can limit scope.

Suggestions for Matching Exercises:

       Keep content uniform.
       Use a larger number of options than questions.
       Avoid trick matches.
       Write clear instructions.
       Make one-to-one matching possible.

3 Suggestions for Short Answer Questions:

   1. Ask direct, concise questions.
   2. Ensure only one correct answer is expected.
   3. Use simple, clear language.

Structure of Short Answer Questions:

       Direct question or incomplete sentence (stem).

       Space for brief student response (usually a word or phrase).

Suggestions for Designing Short Answer Questions:

       Test important concepts.
       Avoid ambiguity.
       Use standard wording for consistent answers.

Five Suggestions for Short Questions:

   1.   Ask for specific information.
   2.   Keep the response brief.
   3.   Use objective scoring criteria.
   4.   Avoid controversial or vague items.
   5.   Place blanks at the end of the sentence when using completion format.

Advantages of Short Questions:

   1. Requires students to produce answers.
   2. Easy to construct.
   3. Reduces guessing compared to MCQs.

Limitations of Short Questions:

   1. May allow for varied responses that complicate scoring.
   2. Not suitable for complex ideas.
   3. May require subjective judgment if not precisely worded.

Uses of Short Answer/Completion Questions:

       Test recall and comprehension.
       Useful for testing vocabulary, grammar, or specific facts.
